transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-14
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Patel (Redwood SE), Sara Alvarez (Nimbus Eng Mgr), Tom Reynolds (Nimbus SRE), Priya Kapoor (Nimbus CTO)
Link to artifacts: deck (https://redwood.app/s/9831/pilot-deck), logs placeholder (gs://nimbus-shared/pilot-9831)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
- Root cause appears correlated with hotkey surge causing KV cache thrash and upstream model queueing; resulted in transient 502/5xx and client retries amplifying pressure.
- Short-term mitigations: adaptive retry budget on client, reduce client retry concurrency, implement soft-fallback routing to a lower-capacity variant under hotkey signature.
- Long-term: KV cache partition hotkey sharding, tokenized request routing, and rate-window smoothing.

Topics covered:
- Incident timeline review (5xx windows)
- KV cache behavior & eviction hypothesis
- Backpressure behavior in serving runtime and request queueing
- Client-side retry patterns and amplification
- Short-term mitigations & pilot config changes
- Next steps: logs, traces, pricing update, profiling session

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: okay everyone, thanks for joining, um, starting the pilot sync for Nimbus Health. main agenda, review the weekend surge, 5xxs and plan mitigations. Liam, you're on the run book side, right?
[00:18] Liam: yea, I'll kick off, thanks. quick context: we saw two main spikes on 2026-10-12 between 02:05 and 03:20 UTC where requests spiked ~6x baseline for a small subset of conversation IDs. that subset hit a hotkey pattern, few prefixes, and the KV cache showed high eviction churn which we think increased tokenization and backend load.
[00:40] Sara: just to be clear, those are real patient-facing requests, so we want minimal retries. latency is more important than cost for us.
[00:51] Priya: agreed, and our SLOs require p99 < 400ms for the routing path, so the 5xxs are a blocker for the pilot ramp.
[01:05] Tom: i pulled the instance metrics, i can share, there were a couple nodes that hit CPU and GPU queue depth high, and then started returning 502s, looks like queue overflow.
[01:20] Liam: right, and to add, when the KV cache misses amplified, the runtime had to fetch longer KV context from storage, which increased processing time per request and caused head-of-line blocking on some worker threads.
[01:38] Speaker 1 (maybe Sara): and we also have a client retry configured at 3 attempts immediate backoff, could be making the load worse.
[01:49] Maya: yeah let's capture that, retry budget and client behaviour is important. Tom, do you have the retry window?
[01:56] Tom: yes, client does 3 immediate retries with no jitter, so in the surge it multiplies the traffic.
[02:08] Liam: that's classic amplification. recommended immediate config: change client to exponential backoff with jitter and cap at 2 retries during pilot; we can also implement a server-side retry budget so we drop non-essential retries.
[02:24] Priya: is there a way to quickly detect the hotkey pattern and route those requests to a dedicated pool?
[02:30] Liam: short-term we can identify hotkey signatures by prefix hashing on the request key and route to a small dedicated shard or to a lower-capacity variant with higher latency tolerance. it's not ideal but quick to deploy.
[02:45] Maya: i'm noting that as a short-term mitigation. longer term we suggested KV partitioning and tokenization changes to smooth hot keys.
[02:56] Sara: the KV cache term, you're saying it's evicting entries quickly so repeated requests miss and re-populate?
[03:04] Liam: exactly — eviction churn. our memory pressure thresholds kicked in, evicted high-value prefixes, and subsequent requests rehydrated the cache causing more downstream work.
[03:18] Tom: i saw the eviction metrics spike around 02:07 UTC, coincident with the first 502 cluster. i can add the exact bucketed numbers to the logs link.
[03:28] Maya: please do. Liam, does the runtime expose per-prefix eviction traces we can turn on?
[03:35] Liam: yes, but it's a bit noisy. i'll instrument a trace that attaches correlation ids so we can see request->evict->miss timeline without massive noise.
[03:45] Tom: perfect.

[04:00] -- discussion about adaptive throttles and rate window smoothing --
[04:03] Liam: another lever: rate-window smoothing at the front door. if we smooth the rate window and add a small token bucket per prefix, we can absorb microbursts and reduce eviction churn.
[04:16] Sara: will that add latency? we can't afford much.
[04:20] Liam: minimal — sub 10ms for token check, but it reduces downstream queuing. you'll trade tiny additional headroom for fewer backend queues.
[04:30] Maya: also worth noting a configurable burst capacity add-on; for pilots we can provision a burst pool that scales for 10 minutes to handle sudden hotkey surges. pricing will reflect that.
[04:43] Priya: can you quantify the cost delta?
[04:46] Maya: i'll send numbers — rough estimate is a 15-25% add-on for short bursts depending on peak TPS.

[05:00] -- customers ask about 5xx taxonomy and whether it's model or infra --
[05:05] Liam: most 5xx were 502/503 from worker queue overflow and some 500s from downstream model container OOM. not a model regression; it's architectural overload.
[05:20] Tom: i did notice one container showed repeated torch/cuda allocation failures around 02:11. that might be an outlier and i will isolate that node's logs.
[05:32] Maya: okay please flag it; if it's a bad instance we should mark it and keep it out of rotation.

[06:00] -- cross talk, fuzzy transcript artifacts --
[06:03] Speaker 2: um we might also look at client-side sharding to spread keys more evenly, but that requires client changes which Nimbus is cautious about.
[06:15] Sara: yes, client changes are possible but we prefer server-side mitigations first.

[06:30] Liam: proposed rapid action plan: (1) instrument per-prefix KV eviction traces; (2) flip client retry to exp backoff w/ jitter + cap to 2 retries; (3) enable a soft-fallback route to a lower-capacity model variant for hotkey signatures; (4) deploy rate-window smoothing and token buckets for hot-key prefixes; (5) schedule profiling to understand queue distributions.
[06:55] Priya: that sounds reasonable. question — fallback variant, will it provide deterministic responses or degrade quality?
[07:04] Liam: it will trade some context length/quality for throughput — think shorter context window or quantized variant. we'll flag accordingly in responses so you can monitor quality regressions.
[07:16] Maya: we also need to discuss telemetry: the console will show per-route p50/p95/p99 and errors but we will add a hotkey dashboard widget for this pilot so you can see per-prefix heatmaps.
[07:30] Sara: yes, heatmap would help triage.

[07:45] -- Incident timeline recap (Tom) --
[07:48] Tom: timeline: 02:05 first surge; 02:07 eviction spike; 02:10 first 502 cluster; 02:11 cuda alloc failures on node-7; 02:20 second spike as retries amplified; by 03:20 traffic normalized.
[08:06] Liam: thanks, that aligns with our server traces. correlating request ids will confirm head-of-line blocking.

[08:20] Sara: one ask — can you expose the request id on error responses so our client side can triage without digging into logs?
[08:28] Maya: yes, we can include a request-id header and a short error code mapping for easier correlation.

[08:40] -- discussion about throttling semantics and client retry budgets --
[08:43] Liam: implement server-side retry budget: when overall queueing surpasses threshold, the server replies 429 with Retry-After for idempotent callers and returns 503 for non-idempotent. combine with client exponential jitter to reduce thundering herd.
[09:00] Priya: we're fine with 429s for non-critical flows but for patient-facing synchronous calls we want clear fallback paths.
[09:10] Maya: okay we'll mark certain endpoints as critical and exempt them from 429s, instead route to fallback variant.

[09:25] -- notes on observability --
[09:28] Liam: i will add a custom metric: hotkey_eviction_ratio and a dashboard alert if it goes above 0.15 for more than 2 minutes.
[09:37] Sara: alert cadence ok — we'll want Slack and pager integration for SRE on-call.

[09:45] -- QA around how quickly config changes can be applied --
[09:48] Maya: most config flips (rate-window smoothing, retry budget) are runtime flags and can be toggled in minutes. shard routing and dedicated pools take longer (hours) to provision.
[10:02] Tom: how about the hotkey dedicated pool — can we pre-create it for the pilot?
[10:07] Liam: yes, we can allocate a tiny shard and route hotkeys there; it's quick if we reuse existing pool images.

[10:20] -- sample log link mention --
[10:23] Tom: i'll upload the per-instance logs and metrics to gs://nimbus-shared/pilot-9831/2026-10-12/ and share link in CRM.
[10:31] Maya: perfect, include time windows and the offending request ids if possible.

[10:40] -- brief discussion of SLA and pricing --
[10:43] Maya: for pilots, recommended default is best-effort hosted with p99 guidance; if you need firm SLOs we recommend the dedicated pilot package with SLA and burst window. i'll include pricing tiers in follow-up.
[10:55] Priya: we'll review internally, our main ask is predictable latency and a plan to prevent future hotkey-induced outages.

[11:05] -- recap and explicit next steps --
[11:08] Maya: recap: (1) Tom uploads logs, (2) Liam instruments eviction traces and dashboard metric, (3) we flip client retries to exp backoff with jitter and cap to 2, (4) Maya sends pricing and burst add-on, (5) schedule deeper profiling session on 2026-10-20. any edits?
[11:30] Sara: sounds good. one more note — we'll run an internal chaos test to validate fallback routing.
[11:38] Liam: recommend doing that after traces are in so you have observability.

[11:50] Maya: thanks everyone. we'll follow up in CRM with links and dates.
[11:55] End of meeting.
